Figure 01 / Budget

Do students with bigger budgets offer more?

Students entered the most they would pay, in extra Canadian dollars, to avoid talking directly about a minor embarrassing situation on campus. The chart pairs that amount with their monthly budget after essentials. The $5 late-arrival and $20 shirt questions each asked for a yes or no.

Larger circles represent more responses at the same two amounts.

Reading the figure

Full study · both groups · 92 respondents

The data give no clear evidence that the amount students would pay rises or falls consistently with their monthly budget (Spearman ρ = 0.138, Holm-adjusted p = 0.376).

Offline preview of the group’s survey results.

Full study · 92 respondents

Key findings.

Naming a price

When students named their own price for avoiding a conversation, 60 of 92 entered $0. The sample gives no clear evidence that students with larger budgets consistently offered more.

Making a choice

For the $20 shirt, 57 of 92 said yes. For the $5 late arrival, 21 of 92 said yes, including 17 of 34 international and 4 of 58 domestic students. Each question changed both the price and the situation.

Describing a feeling

Students who gave a high rating for one feeling tended to rate the others higher too. Across all three items, internal consistency was 0.793 on Cronbach’s alpha measure. These hypothetical answers cannot tell us whether those feelings or student status caused a payment choice.

Study notes

Who answered?

The dataset contains 92 complete responses, including 58 domestic and 34 international students.

How to interpret these results

The proposal targeted the two Fall 2026 STA304 lecture sections at UTM and planned recruitment through Piazza by student status. Random selection within each group could not be verified. The results describe these respondents’ hypothetical choices. The two payment scenarios change both the price and the situation, so their difference cannot identify a price effect.

Methods and sources

The group’s final exploratory analysis used Spearman rank correlation for the two amounts, two-proportion z-tests for the scenarios, and Cronbach’s alpha for the three ratings. Its significance decisions used a Holm adjustment across 14 comparisons. For late arrival, 4 of 58 domestic respondents said yes. Under the hypothesis of equal payment rates, the smallest of the four expected counts was 7.76. A separate check using two-sided Fisher exact tests for the two scenarios and the same 14-test Holm adjustment also found a group difference for late arrival.

Source: The Significant Five’s cleaned survey, codebook, original proposal, and final exploratory data analysis (25 October 2026). All amounts are in Canadian dollars.
